title: Hallucination to truth: a review of fact-checking and factuality evaluation in large language models
abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast and diverse internet corpora that often include inaccurate or misleading content. Consequently, LLMs can generate misinformation, making robust fact-checking essential. This review systematically analyzes how LLM-generated content is evaluated for factual accuracy by exploring key challenges such as hallucinations, dataset limitations, and the reliability of evaluation metrics. The review emphasizes the need for strong fact-checking frameworks that integrate advanced prompting strategies, domain-specific fine-tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods. It proposes five research questions that guide the analysis of the recent literature from 2020 to 2025, focusing on evaluation methods and mitigation techniques. Instruction tuning, multi-agent reasoning, and RAG frameworks for external knowledge access are also reviewed. The key findings demonstrate the limitations of current metrics, the importance of validated external evidence, and the improvement of factual consistency through domain-specific customization. The review underscores the importance of building more accurate, understandable, and context-aware fact-checking. These insights contribute to the advancement of research toward more trustworthy models.

claims.text: A fine-tuned BERT model achieved a 76.5% F1-score on the GossipCop dataset, outperforming GPT-3.5-turbo which scored 70.2%.
A supervised RoBERTa-Base classifier achieved a 52.9% F1-macro score on the FA-KES dataset, outperforming zero-shot GPT-3.5-turbo at 43.3%.
A fine-tuned BioBERT model achieved 80.2% accuracy on the CliniFact dataset, outperforming Llama3-70B which achieved 53.6% accuracy when fine-tuned.
The MiniCheck-FT5 model fine-tuned on synthetic data achieved a 74.7% Balanced Accuracy on the LLM-AGGREFACT benchmark.
The Hierarchical Step-by-Step (HiSS) prompting method achieved an F1-score of 53.9% on the RAWFC dataset, compared to 44.4% for vanilla Chain-of-Thought.
Integrating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with GPT-4 increased accuracy on non-ambiguous PolitiFact claims from 75% to 89%.
The Fact-Check-Then-RAG method improved Llama 3 70B accuracy on the PubMedQA dataset from 60.60% to 73.60%.

limitations.text: The scope of the review is inherently constrained by the rapid velocity of technological innovation within the LLM domain, meaning emerging preprint findings and proprietary model advancements may not be fully encapsulated.
Currently used lexical and semantic overlap evaluation metrics quantify surface-level similarity rather than factual consistency, rendering them less effective at detecting nuanced errors.
The majority of existing fact-checking benchmark datasets either lack the realistic complexity of real-world claims and are domain-independent or are too narrow to be generalized.

future_work.text: Development of multi-dimensional evaluation frameworks with standardized metrics for explainability and interpretability that correlate with human cognitive trust.
Proactive prevention of factual hallucinations by optimizing RAG systems for complex information environments and enabling dynamic knowledge updates within LLM architectures.
Integration of formal verification methods and symbolic reasoning to enhance the logical consistency of LLMs on multi-hop and complex inferential claims.
Expansion of LLM fact-checking to robust multimodal verification and low-resource multilingual contexts.

methodologies.name: Systematic Literature Review Protocol
methodologies.description: A multi-phase review methodology comprising planning, multi-database search across Web of Science, arXiv, Scopus, and OpenReview, title/abstract screening, full-text evaluation, and categorization across five target research questions.
conditions: Publication window from January 1, 2021 to September 15, 2025
Multi-stage screening yielding 64 selected core articles published between September 2022 and August 2025
